/-!
# Erdős Problem 479

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/479](https://www.erdosproblems.com/479)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos479

/--
Is it true that, for every integer $k\neq 1$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that
$2^n\equiv k\pmod{n}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_479 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (k : ℤ) (k ≠ 1),
    { n : ℕ | (2 : ℤ) ^ n ≡ k [ZMOD (n : ℤ)] }.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos479

reformulations.difference: The extended binder elaborates to `∀ (k₀ k : ℤ), k ≠ 1 → ...`, with an unused outer integer quantifier. The solution set also ranges over all natural numbers, whereas the linked note explicitly defines A(k) using n ≥ 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The unused quantifier can be removed because ℤ is inhabited. At n = 0, integer congruence modulo zero becomes equality, so the condition is 1 = k, impossible under k ≠ 1. Thus, for every permitted k, the solution set is exactly the positive-natural solution set. The combined equivalence was proved as `rhs_equiv_positive_n` in /workspace/review/scratch.lean without using the admitted problem theorem. Removing n = 1 also preserves infinitude, as separately proved there.
